package_info.why_malicious: The package is not intentionally malicious, but contains multiple critical deserialization vulnerabilities (notably in versions prior to 2.9.9.2) that allow attackers to exploit unsafe polymorphic type handling and improper input validation. These flaws enable remote code execution, information disclosure, and other severe impacts when untrusted data is deserialized.

execution_context.file_location: jackson-databind core library (Java classpath, typically in application dependencies)
required_permissions: network (if deserialized objects initiate network connections)
environment_vars (if deserialized objects access environment variables)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
Object obj = mapper.readValue(untrustedInput, Object.class);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Deserializes untrusted data using Jackson's ObjectMapper without type restrictions, which can trigger instantiation of attacker-supplied classes and execution of their methods, potentially leading to remote code execution or sensitive data access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing untrusted input without restricting allowed types enables attackers to supply crafted payloads that exploit known gadget chains, resulting in arbitrary code execution or unauthorized access to system resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is that deserialization only instantiates safe, explicitly allowed types. Vulnerable versions allow attacker-controlled types, violating the principle of least privilege and safe deserialization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use involves deserializing trusted, validated data from known sources, with strict type whitelisting or input validation to prevent instantiation of arbitrary classes.
key_indicators: Deserialization of untrusted data using ObjectMapper.readValue()
No use of enableDefaultTyping or type whitelisting
Absence of input validation or type restriction mechanisms

execution_context.file_location: jackson-databind core library (Java classpath, within application dependency tree)
required_permissions: network (if gadget classes initiate network connections)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Allows attackers to specify arbitrary classes in input data via polymorphic type handling (e.g., @JsonTypeInfo with Id.CLASS), enabling exploitation of gadget classes for remote code execution or other malicious actions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Improper input validation and unsafe polymorphic type handling (e.g., enabling @JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS without type whitelisting) are classic vectors for deserialization attacks, as they allow attackers to instantiate arbitrary classes from input.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is to restrict polymorphic deserialization to a safe, explicitly defined set of types. Vulnerable configurations allow attacker-controlled types, breaking this security boundary.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Polymorphic deserialization is legitimate if types are strictly controlled via type whitelisting or custom deserializers.
key_indicators: No type whitelisting or restriction on deserialized types
Use of jackson-databind versions prior to 2.9.9.2
References to known gadget classes in input data
Presence of CVEs such as CVE-2018-1000873, CVE-2018-14721, CVE-2019-14379

attack_chain.action: Application receives untrusted input (e.g., JSON) and passes it to jackson-databind for deserialization without type restrictions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Deserialization of attacker-controlled data, allowing attacker to specify types/classes instantiated by the application.

attack_chain.action: Vulnerable jackson-databind version mishandles polymorphic type information, allowing instantiation of arbitrary classes or execution of gadget chains supplied by the attacker.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution, information disclosure, or other malicious actions depending on the capabilities of the instantiated gadget classes.

behavioral_signatures: Deserialization of untrusted data using ObjectMapper.readValue() or similar APIs in vulnerable jackson-databind versions (<2.9.9.2)
Polymorphic type handling with @JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS) or enableDefaultTyping without explicit type whitelisting
Absence of input validation or type restriction mechanisms in deserialization logic
Instantiation of unexpected or dangerous classes during deserialization
file_indicators: Dependencies on com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind with version <2.9.9.2 in build files (pom.xml, build.gradle, etc.)
Source code using ObjectMapper.readValue() or enableDefaultTyping() without type whitelisting
Presence of @JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS) annotations without type restriction
network_indicators: Outbound network connections initiated immediately after deserialization operations (may indicate gadget exploitation)
Unusual network activity from application processes following deserialization of untrusted input
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan project dependencies for com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind versions earlier than 2.9.9.2. Audit source code for deserialization of untrusted data using ObjectMapper.readValue(), enableDefaultTyping(), or @JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS) without explicit type whitelisting. Monitor runtime for instantiation of unexpected classes during deserialization and for abnormal network or filesystem activity following deserialization events. Flag any use of polymorphic typing without strict type controls.
